title: Displays, pixels & panels
summary: Separate panel technology from display settings.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: A display’s resolution describes its pixel grid, while its refresh rate describes how often it can update the image each second. These are independent characteristics. A high-resolution panel can still run at a modest refresh rate. Pixel density relates the number of pixels to physical size, which affects perceived sharpness. Color gamut describes the range of colors a display can reproduce rather than how many pixels it contains.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: LCD panels use a backlight and a liquid-crystal layer to control transmitted light. OLED pixels emit their own light, allowing very dark black regions when pixels are off. IPS, TN, and VA are LCD panel approaches with different viewing-angle, response, and contrast tradeoffs. A digitizer detects touch input; a visible image with unresponsive touch can therefore involve a separate input component. Before replacing a screen, verify the source, cable, supported resolution, and refresh settings using a known-good connection.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
